source: Plain-English versions written for DKLA by an agent swarm and checked by a legal checker; they explain the narrative, they are not the court's words.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Tompkins claimed longstanding open use made him a licensee entitled to ordinary care.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Tompkins said that because people had openly walked this path for years, he was there with the railroad’s tacit permission (a “licensee”), not trespassing. If so, the railroad owed him ordinary, reasonable care, and it would be liable if it had simply been careless.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Erie, a New York corporation, argued that Pennsylvania decisions treated users of a longitudinal railroad path as trespassers, owed only protection against willful or wanton harm while undiscovered.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Erie answered that Pennsylvania’s courts treated people walking along (not across) the tracks as trespassers. A railroad that had not noticed a trespasser only had to avoid hurting him deliberately or recklessly, so mere carelessness would not make Erie liable.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: He further argued that without a Pennsylvania statute, railroad duty was general law on which a federal court could exercise independent judgment.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Tompkins also argued that, because no Pennsylvania statute covered the railroad’s duty, the question was “general law” under Swift v. Tyson. That would let the federal court decide for itself what care the railroad owed, instead of following Pennsylvania’s court decisions.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The issue was whether a diversity court could bypass authoritative state decisions on a substantive state-created claim.
cp-erie-decision.plain: The question was whether a federal court, hearing the case only because the parties were from different states, could ignore what a state’s highest courts had said about a claim that state law itself created.

cp-garcia.sentence: Hilton moved to dismiss because Garcia had not expressly alleged publication to another person and because the accusation was conditionally privileged.
cp-garcia.plain: Hilton asked the court to throw the case out for two reasons. Garcia’s complaint never said outright that the accusation was told to anyone else, which a defamation claim needs. And Hilton said the accusation was covered by a limited (“conditional”) privilege that protects some statements made in good faith.

cp-garcia.sentence: Hilton therefore had to assert conditional privilege as an affirmative defense rather than obtain dismissal merely because it might be available.
cp-garcia.plain: So the chance that the privilege might protect Hilton was not enough to end the case at the start. Hilton had to raise the privilege itself, as a defense in its answer, and the court would decide later whether it really applied.
